chapters.title: Before There Was Light, God Spoke

narration.text: One bite of one fruit, in the one place on earth where nothing was wrong.
Ten generations later, the Maker of that garden would grieve that He had made man at all.
The text calls that first world very good. Then, step by step, it shows us how it came apart.
How does a very good world come to that? And who would still be standing when it did?
I keep the old stories. Tonight I will tell you one of them, whole.
Most readers see seven separate tales here. The text tells only one story.
Stay to the end, and you will see the small word that saves it.
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Before any city, any king or any name, there was only the deep, and the dark over it.
And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.
No struggle, no rival, no battle with the sea. He speaks, and it happens.
Day after day the world fills: sky, then sea and land, then the lights, then everything that swims and flies and walks.
And each day ends the same way, with one quiet word over it: good.
And the earth was without form and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep.
Formless and empty. In the days that follow He shapes what had no form and fills what was empty, one day at a time.
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Not a servant made to feed the gods, as the old nations said. An image. A face that reflects His.
And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.
Very good. Remember those two words. The rest of this story is the long road away from them, and the question is whether anyone finds the way back.
Then on the seventh day He rests. Not because He is tired, but because the work is finished. How long could it stay this way?
And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Dust and breath. The lowest thing on the ground, and the closest thing to God.
And the Lord God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.
A garden, not a palace. Rivers, trees, work to do, and nothing to fear in any of it.
Notice what he is given first. Not a temple, not a throne, but work: to dress the garden and to keep it.
And a name for every living creature. The animals come to him one by one, and he names them all.
Eden means delight. A river flows out of it and parts into four great heads, and the land around it holds gold.
One tree. Every other tree was theirs. One command, with a reason given: in the day you eat it, you die.
And the Lord God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.
God brings the woman to the man the way a father brings a bride. The first wedding is in a garden, with God as the witness.
The first words a man speaks in the Bible are a song about another person.
Two people, one garden, nothing hidden between them. And in the shade of one tree, something was listening.
Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the Lord God had made.
It does not attack. It does not lie, at first. It asks a question.
Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?
Every tree? No. One tree. But the question makes the gift sound small and the rule sound cruel.
Notice what she adds. God never said do not touch it. The rule is already growing in her mind, and so is the doubt.
And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die:
For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.
The oldest lie is not that God does not exist. It is that He is holding something back from you.
She looks at the tree again. Good for food. Pleasant to the eyes. Something to make one wise. Every reason sounds good.
The serpent never forces her hand. It only reframes the one command, until the giver of the garden looks like the enemy.
She is not foolish, and she is not weak. She is talked out of trusting the one who gave her everything she has.
she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.
He was with her. The whole time, standing right there beside her. He said nothing, and he ate.
And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked;
Their eyes were opened, just as promised. And the first thing they saw was shame. Then they heard Him coming.
Notice who comes looking. Not the guilty pair searching for God, but God Himself walking in the garden, calling out a question.
Then comes the blame. The man points at the woman, and, if you listen closely, he points at God Himself as well. Who gave her to him?
Three people, three excuses. The man blames the woman, the woman blames the serpent, and no one simply says, I did it.
The serpent is cursed to crawl in the dust. But inside that curse there is a promise, almost hidden, the first good news in the whole Bible.
it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.
Even here there is mercy. Before they go, He makes them coats of skins with His own hands.
So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way,
Then comes a strange line: the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil, and he must not stay.
They walk out east, into thorns and sweat and a hard world that fights back. And outside the garden, Eve gives birth to two sons.
And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.
Two brothers, born outside the garden. One follows the flock across the hills. The other works the cursed ground with his hands.
In time, both bring an offering. Cain brings fruit of the ground. Abel brings the firstlings of his flock, the best he has.
And the Lord had respect unto Abel and to his offering:
Why one and not the other? The text does not say the gift was wrong. It says the Lord looked at Abel first, and then at his gift.
But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.
And then God does something remarkable. He comes to Cain before anything has happened, and warns him.
Sin is pictured like an animal crouching at a door, waiting to be let in. Cain can still rule over it. He does not.
and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.
No one tells us what they said out in that field. The text goes quiet, and the silence is the worst part.
The first death in the Bible is not old age. It is a brother's hand. Then the question comes.
And the Lord said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother’s keeper?
His answer is the first lie told to God's face, and the first time a man refuses to stand by his own brother.
Cain goes out from the presence of the Lord, east again, further from the garden than his parents ever went.
Adam and Eve have lost both sons in one day. The world outside Eden is getting darker. And yet, far down the family line, one man walks the other way.
Generations pass. Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared. Names, ages, and then the same three words, over and over again: and he died.
Except once. One man in that long list breaks the pattern completely.
And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.
No death notice. Only a walk. He walked with God so long that one day he simply did not come home.
Enoch lived three hundred and sixty five years, a short life for those days. But the text measures him by one thing only: he walked.
Enoch's son is Methuselah, the oldest man who ever lived. His long years run out in the very year the flood comes.
It is possible, the text says, to walk with God in a dark age. Soon that will be tested, because the world is about to fill with violence.
Ten generations after Eden, the earth is full of people, and full of noise. Cities of tents cover the plains, and nobody looks up.
And God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.
The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence.
And then comes a line most readers rush past. The text does not say He was angry first.
The strong take what they want, and the weak learn to hide. Brothers turn on brothers, just as Cain did, only now it is everyone.
And it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.
Grieved. At His heart. The Maker of that very good world, hurting over what His people became. And then He spoke.
Not man alone. The beasts of the field, the creeping things, the birds of the air. Everything that breathes on the dry land.
It sounds like the end of the whole story. But in the middle of all that violence, one small word changes everything that follows.
But Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord.
Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God.
Walked with God. The same words as Enoch. The thread survived.
Noah, a just man in a violent age. Not perfect in the sense of sinless, but whole, undivided, the same man in the dark as in the light.
And Noah begat three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
One man and his family, walking the other way while the whole world ran past them.
Notice how the text counts the fall, one step at a time.
A fruit taken. A brother killed. Then violence filling the whole earth.
Each generation opened the door a little wider, until no one even remembered there had been a door.
But read the order carefully. Before the judgment comes the grief, and before the flood comes grace.
Look at how each sin grows. In the garden, a bite and a hidden face. In the field, a brother's blood. By Noah's day, the whole earth.
And notice the mercy at every step. Coats of skin for the exiles. A mark of protection on Cain. A warning long before the flood.
Judgment is real in these chapters. But it never comes without a warning.
Every step down that slope began with a voice saying God holds back.
The flood is not the story of a cold God, but a wounded heart.
And the word that saves the story is small. But. But Noah found grace.
Noah did not climb out of that world. He simply kept walking with God.
Put the chapters side by side and they rhyme. A garden lost, a field of blood, a world of violence, and every time a voice asking where.
Grace was not a reward for Noah. Grace found him first, then he walked.
Would you have walked against that crowd? Tell me in the comments below.
Next on the channel, Noah builds the ark, and the whole valley laughs.
